As well as working in data visualisation, I'm also a researcher at Massey University. Most of my research focuses on understanding the sources and transmission pathways of antibiotic resistant bacteria such as \*Escherichia coli\*. I recently discovered a tool for drawing plasmid maps in R. This blog is mainly for people who work with plasmid sequence data. I'll run through how I drew plasmid maps in R using the [plasmapR package](https://bradyajohnston.github.io/plasmapR/) (written by Brady Johnston). I found the default map too busy, and I wanted control over which genes were labelled and the colours used, so I modified the ggplot object that plasmapR returns. I'll start by drawing a map for a single plasmid, then show how to draw maps for multiple plasmids. You can download the plasmid sequence [here](https://github.com/sburgess2/blogs/tree/main/2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data).

The plasmid sequence originates from an *Escherichia coli* strain isolated from dairy cattle faeces. The plasmid was assembled using Flye and annotated using Prokka as described in [Burgess et al. (2021)](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.idairyj.2021.104998).

## Packages

plasmapR isn't on CRAN, so it needs to be installed from GitHub.

```{r}
#| eval: false

devtools::install_github("bradyajohnston/plasmapr")
```

First load the libraries we'll be using.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(plasmapR)
library(ggrepel)
```

### Reading in the data

Next read the GenBank file into the plasmid object with `read_gb()`.

```{r}
fl <- "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/data/pEE072d2.gb"
plasmid <- fl |> read_gb()
```

Then we can convert the plasmid object into a data frame using `as.data.frame()`.

```{r}
df <- plasmid |>
  as.data.frame()
```

Here are the first six rows of this data frame:

```{r}
head(df)
```

### Grouping the genes by category

This data frame contains three types of features. The source:

```{r}
df |> filter(type == "source")
```

The miscellaneous features:

```{r}
df |> filter(type == "misc_feature")
```

The coding sequences (CDS), showing the first ten rows:

```{r}
df |>
  filter(type == "CDS") |>
  head(10)
```

We will keep only the CDS.

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  filter(type == "CDS")
```

Next, we'll use `mutate()` and `case_when()` to add a column called `annotation`, which will group each gene into a category (ESBL, Plasmid transfer, Hypothetical protein, and Other), based on the gene name. `case_when()` works through the conditions in order and stops at the first match, so the order matters. The `str_detect()` function is used to look for a pattern (in this case certain gene names) in a string (in this case the `name` column). Any names starting with "EE0072d" are grouped as "Hypothetical protein". Some *tra* genes are also labelled as hypothetical proteins (e.g. "traG (Yi 2010) hypothetical protein CDS"), so `"^tra.*hypothetical"` puts these in the same group. This line comes before the "Plasmid transfer" line, otherwise `"^tra"` would group these genes as "Plasmid transfer" first. Anything not matched ends up as "Other".

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  mutate(
    annotation = case_when(
      str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
      str_detect(name, "^EE0072d|^tra.*hypothetical") ~ "Hypothetical protein",
      str_detect(name, "^tra") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    name = name |>
      str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
      str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
      str_remove(" .*$")
  )
```

The *bla*~CTX-M~ gene is named *bla_1* in the annotation, so I used `str_replace()` to rename it to *bla*~CTX-M~ for the map label. Prokka also adds a number to the end of repeated gene names (e.g. *traI_1*, *traI_2*), so `str_remove()` drops the underscore and the one or two digits that follow it.

The pattern `"_\\d{1,2}$"` is a regular expression (regex), and it can be read piece by piece:

- `_` matches an underscore.
- `\\d` matches any digit (0 to 9).
- `{1,2}` means one to two of the thing before it, so `\\d{1,2}` matches one or two digits.
- `$` means the end of the string (whereas \^ means the beginning of a string), so the match only happens when the underscore and digits are the last thing in the name.

Put together, the pattern only matches an underscore followed by one or two digits at the very end of a name. This means *traI_1* becomes *traI*, but the locus tags (e.g. EE0072d_05113) are left alone, because they have five digits after the underscore.

Regex is tricky to learn (I definitely struggle with it). AI is great for writing regex. [This cheatsheet](https://rstudio.github.io/cheatsheets/html/strings.html) is also helpful for learning how to manipulate strings using the `stringr` package and regex.

Some of the *tra* genes also have long names, such as "traG (Yi 2010) hypothetical protein CDS". To keep just the gene name, the last `str_remove()` uses the pattern `" .*$"`:

- The space at the start matches the first space in the name.
- `.` matches any character.
- `*` means zero or more of the thing before it, so `.*` matches any run of characters.
- `$` means the end of the string.

Together, the pattern matches everything from the first space to the end of the name, so "traG (Yi 2010) hypothetical protein CDS" becomes *traG*.

Next, we need to select the columns `plot_plasmid()` expects:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction)
```

We also need to add a `mid` column (the midpoint of each gene), which is used later to position the gene labels.

```{r}
#| eval: false

df |>
  mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)
```

We can then chain the code above together and save it into a new object, `df1`.

```{r}
df1 <- df |>
  filter(type == "CDS") |>
  mutate(
    annotation = case_when(
      str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
      str_detect(name, "^EE0072d|^tra.*hypothetical") ~ "Hypothetical protein",
      str_detect(name, "^tra") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
      TRUE ~ "Other"
    ),
    name = name |>
      str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
      str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
      str_remove(" .*$")
  ) |>
  select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction) |>
  mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)
```

I wanted all the genes to be visible on the map, so I kept the "Other" genes. If you don't want them displayed on the plasmid map, you could filter them out using:

```{r}
#| eval: false

df1 |>
  filter_out(type == "Other")
```

### The layers of a plasmid plot

`plot_plasmid()` returns a ggplot object. Here's the default map.

```{r}
pl1 <- df1 |> plot_plasmid()
pl1
```

The default map labels every gene, which gets crowded. After a lot of playing around, I realised that removing some of the layers was the key to getting the map into a format I liked more. The plot is built from layers, which are stored as a list in `pl1$layers`.

```{r}
pl1$layers
```

There are five layers. Layer 1 draws the plasmid backbone (the ring), and layer 3 draws the gene arrows. These are the two layers I kept. Layers 2, 4, and 5 are the `geom_label_repel()` labels, the `geom_fit_text()` text, and the `annotate()` layer. To see what each layer adds, we'll remove them one at a time.

Removing only layer 1 drops the plasmid backbone, leaving the gene arrows and labels without the ring.

```{r}
pl_no_backbone <- pl1
pl_no_backbone$layers <- pl_no_backbone$layers[-1]
pl_no_backbone
```

Removing only layer 2 drops the `geom_label_repel()` labels, which sit outside the ring with lines pointing to each gene.

```{r}
pl_no_repel <- pl1
pl_no_repel$layers <- pl_no_repel$layers[-2]
pl_no_repel
```

Removing only layer 3 drops the gene arrows, leaving the ring and labels without the genes.

```{r}
pl_no_arrows <- pl1
pl_no_arrows$layers <- pl_no_arrows$layers[-3]
pl_no_arrows
```

Removing only layer 4 drops the `geom_fit_text()` text, which fits some of the gene names inside the arrows (when the arrows are long enough).

```{r}
pl_no_fit_text <- pl1
pl_no_fit_text$layers <- pl_no_fit_text$layers[-4]
pl_no_fit_text
```

Removing only layer 5 drops the `annotate()` layer, which adds text to the centre of the map. If you want to keep the plasmid name and length of your plasmid then keep this layer in.

```{r}
pl_no_annotate <- pl1
pl_no_annotate$layers <- pl_no_annotate$layers[-5]
pl_no_annotate
```

Now that we know what each layer does, we can remove the second, fourth, and fifth layers from `pl1`.

```{r}
pl1$layers <- pl1$layers[-c(2, 4, 5)]
```

### Choosing the colours

Where I can, I like to select colours that are relevant to my topic. Given this plasmid contains an antimicrobial resistance gene, I decided to use some of the colours from these two World Antimicrobial Resistance Awareness Week images.

![](images/AMR-Poster.jpg){width="45%"} ![](images/amr-is-invisible-banner-en.jpg){width="50%"}

\[Missing: source and credit for the two images\]

I uploaded them to <https://imagecolorpicker.com/> to get the hex codes for the two shades of blue from the first image, and the orange from the second image. I used the light blue for the "Other" genes and a light grey for the hypothetical proteins so they're in the background.

We'll use these colours to create a custom palette as follows:

```{r}
custom_colors <- c(
  "Plasmid transfer" = "#1898d5",
  "ESBL" = "#fe6f43",
  "Other" = "#cbe8f6",
  "Hypothetical protein" = "#D9D9D9"
)
```

### Building the final plasmid plot

I only wanted the ESBL and plasmid transfer genes labelled. To do this, we'll add our own `geom_text_repel()` layer from the ggrepel package that keeps just those two groups. Each label starts at the midpoint of its gene and is nudged out from the ring, and `geom_text_repel()` pushes overlapping labels apart. Setting `min.segment.length = Inf` stops it drawing lines from the labels to the genes. `append(..., after = 0)` adds the new text layer as the first layer. Setting `inherit.aes = FALSE` stops the text layer inheriting the aesthetics from the plasmapR layers.

```{r}
pl1_modified <- pl1
pl1_modified$layers <- append(
  pl1_modified$layers,
  geom_text_repel(
    data = df1 |>
      filter(type %in% c("ESBL", "Plasmid transfer")),
    aes(x = mid, y = 3, label = name),
    inherit.aes = FALSE,
    size = 3,
    color = "black",
    nudge_y = 0.6,
    min.segment.length = Inf,
    show.legend = FALSE
  ),
  after = 0
)
pl1_modified$layers
```

Finally, we'll add the custom colours, remove the background and axes with `theme_void()`, and rename the legend.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-height: 8

custom_plot <- pl1_modified +
  scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
  theme_void() +
  theme(legend.position = "top") +
  labs(fill = "Gene category")

custom_plot
```

Any further manipulation (e.g. lining up some of the gene names with the genes a bit better) I do in Inkscape.

## Drawing maps for multiple plasmids

If you have more than one plasmid, you can wrap the steps above in a function. In the example below, `make_plasmid_map()` has one argument, `fl`, which is the file path to a GenBank file. It's best to get the map looking right for one plasmid first, then copy the code into the body of the function.

```{r}
#| eval: false

make_plasmid_map <- function(fl) {
  df1 <- fl |>
    read_gb() |>
    as.data.frame() |>
    filter(type == "CDS") |>
    mutate(
      annotation = case_when(
        str_detect(name, "^bla") ~ "ESBL",
        str_detect(name, "^EE0072d|^tra.*hypothetical") ~ "Hypothetical protein",
        str_detect(name, "^tra") ~ "Plasmid transfer",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      name = name |>
        str_replace("bla_1", "blaCTX-M") |>
        str_remove("_\\d{1,2}$") |>
        str_remove(" .*$")
    ) |>
    select(index, name, type = annotation, start, end, direction) |>
    mutate(mid = (start + end) / 2)

  pl <- df1 |> plot_plasmid()
  pl$layers <- pl$layers[-c(2, 4, 5)]
  pl$layers <- append(
    pl$layers,
    geom_text_repel(
      data = df1 |>
        filter(type %in% c("ESBL", "Plasmid transfer")),
      aes(x = mid, y = 3, label = name),
      inherit.aes = FALSE,
      size = 3,
      color = "black",
      nudge_y = 0.6,
      min.segment.length = Inf,
      show.legend = FALSE
    ),
    after = 0
  )

  pl +
    scale_fill_manual(values = custom_colors) +
    theme_void() +
    theme(legend.position = "top") +
    labs(fill = "Gene category")
}
```

Rather than typing out each file path, we can use `list.files()` to find every GenBank file in a folder. `pattern = "\\.gb$"` keeps only files ending in .gb(if your files end in .gb, like the example plasmid, use `"\\.gb$"` instead), and `full.names = TRUE` returns the full path rather than just the file name. You can then use `map()` from purrr to run the function over the file paths, which returns a list of maps.

```{r}
#| eval: false

gb_files <- list.files("data/plasmids/", pattern = "\\.gb$", full.names = TRUE)

maps <- gb_files |> map(make_plasmid_map)
```

To put the maps side by side, we can use the patchwork package, which combines ggplot objects into a single figure. `wrap_plots()` takes a list of plots, and `plot_layout(guides = "collect")` keeps a single shared legend rather than one per map.

```{r}
#| eval: false

library(patchwork)

wrap_plots(maps) +
  plot_layout(guides = "collect")
```

For two maps, you can also add them together directly with `maps[[1]] + maps[[2]]`.

## Saving the figure

Finally, you can save the map as an SVG, so you can make further changes in a vector graphics editor such as Inkscape. To save as an SVG, `ggsave()` needs the svglite package, so install it first if you don't already have it.

```{r}
#| eval: false

install.packages("svglite")
```

```{r}
#| eval: false

ggsave(
  plot = custom_plot,
  filename = "2026/2026-10-10-plasmidmap/output/plasmid_map.svg",
  width = 210,
  height = 148,
  units = "mm"
)
```

## Key tips

- `plot_plasmid()` returns a ggplot object, so you can remove, reorder, or add layers (`pl1$layers`) and change layer parameters directly when the defaults don't quite fit.

- The order of the conditions in `case_when()` matters. The most specific groups should go first.

- It's easier to get the map right for one plasmid before wrapping the code in a function.
